t:
(a) Design Requirements.—
        (1) In general.—The design of the coins minted under this Act shall be emblematic of the life and legacy of Mark Twain. 
        (2) Designation and inscriptions.—On each coin minted under this Act there shall be—
            (A) a designation of the value of the coin; 
            (B) an inscription of the year “2016”; and 
            (C) inscriptions of the words “Liberty”, “In God We Trust”, “United States of America”, and “E Pluribus Unum”.   
    (b) Selection.—The design for the coins minted under this Act shall be—
        (1) selected by the Secretary after consultation with the Commission of Fine Arts and the Board of the Mark Twain House and Museum; and 
        (2) reviewed by the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee.

fable.w: Before selecting the coin design, the Secretary must consult the Board of the Mark Twain House and Museum, a private nonprofit outside the federal government, and the design must be reviewed by the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee, an advisory body that includes members of the public. The tempting reading is that this is only intra-government coordination because the Commission of Fine Arts is a federal body, but the museum board and the citizen advisory committee bring outside parties into the federal design decision.
fable.s:

qwen_block.w: The section requires the Secretary to consult with the Commission of Fine Arts and the Board of the Mark Twain House and Museum before selecting the coin design. The Commission of Fine Arts is an advisory body composed of non-federal experts, and the Board of the Mark Twain House and Museum is a non-profit organization outside the federal government. This consultation with outside parties constitutes participation.
qwen_block.s: selected by the Secretary after consultation with the Commission of Fine Arts and the Board of the Mark Twain House and Museum

opus.w: Before the Secretary makes a federal decision (choosing the coin design), the Secretary must consult the Board of the Mark Twain House and Museum, a private nonprofit outside the federal government. The Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee, which includes public members, also reviews the design. It would be wrong to read this as consultation only within the government: the Commission of Fine Arts is federal, but the museum board is not.
opus.s: selected by the Secretary after consultation with the Commission of Fine Arts and the Board of the Mark Twain House and Museum
opus.b:
1. **Step 1:** The tempting wrong reading is that this is only consultation between federal bodies. The Commission of Fine Arts is a federal agency, so consulting it alone would not count. But the Secretary must also consult the Board of the Mark Twain House and Museum before selecting the design. That museum is a private nonprofit in Hartford, so this consultation crosses the federal boundary. The design is also reviewed by the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee, which includes members of the public.

2. **Step 2:**

qwen_chat.w: The section requires the Secretary to consult with the Commission of Fine Arts, the Board of the Mark Twain House and Museum, and the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee before selecting the coin design. The Commission of Fine Arts and the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee are advisory bodies composed of outside experts and citizens, and the Mark Twain House and Museum is a private non-profit organization. These entities are outside the federal government, satisfying the definition of participation.
qwen_chat.s: selected by the Secretary after consultation with the Commission of Fine Arts and the Board of the Mark Twain House and Museum; and (2) reviewed by the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the Commission of Fine Arts and the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee are federal entities or composed of federal employees, thus making this intra-governmental coordination. However, the Commission of Fine Arts is an independent advisory body composed of experts in the arts (outside the executive branch), and the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee is explicitly named as "Citizens," implying non-federal members. Furthermore, the Board of the Mark Twain House and Museum is a private non-profit organization. Therefore, the consultation involves parties outside the federal government.
